talks.title: Krzysztof Dziamski - New Dimension of War: Cyberwarfare Between Israel and Hamas
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Krzysztof Dziamski - New Dimension of War: Cyberwarfare Between Israel and Hamas.
talks.summary:
Overview: Krzysztof Dziamski presents at CONFidence on cyberwarfare between Israel and Hamas, analyzing how cyber operations fit within the broader kinetic conflict timeline.

Key Topics: October 7, 2023 attack and subsequent military operations; cyber operations as supporting rather than decisive warfare elements; timeline of Israeli, US, UK, and regional responses; and intelligence aspects of the conflict.

Technical Details: Dziamski maps cyber events against kinetic military operations from October 2023 through 2024, including Israeli strikes on Iranian embassy in Syria and operations in Gaza, analyzing how cyber capabilities supported conventional military objectives.

Takeaways: Cyberwarfare remains adjunct to kinetic operations in modern conflicts. Analysts should study cyber events within full geopolitical context rather than treating them as independent domains.

talks.title: Tomasz Cholewa - Hack your Kubernetes cluster and secure it properly
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Tomasz Cholewa - Hack your Kubernetes cluster and secure it properly.
talks.summary:
Kubernetes Exposure Context

Tomasz Cholewa frames the talk from a worried Kubernetes user’s perspective, noting AI workloads increasingly run on clusters where security often lags adoption. He revisits a recent Wiz finding in the widely used Ingress NGINX controller that alarmed organizations after his earlier presentation.

Ingress NGINX Exploit Chain

Ingress NGINX exposes an unauthenticated admission webhook endpoint reachable from pods. Attackers craft malicious admission reviews using dangerous annotations, upload oversized files to create temporary filesystem artifacts, then probe file descriptors to recover deleted content and load a malicious shared library into the controller container.

Privilege Impact and Mitigation

Because Ingress NGINX’s RBAC can read secrets cluster-wide, demonstrated exploits retrieve secrets from all namespaces—He cites that over 40% of organizations use this controller for its maturity and annotation extensibility. Cholewa urges upgrading patched controller versions and reviewing assumptions behind the attack prerequisites.

talks.title: Thomas Fischer - Car Hacking: Two Decades of Evolution and Exploitation
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Thomas Fischer - Car Hacking: Two Decades of Evolution and Exploitation.
talks.summary:
Twenty years of car hacking

Thomas Fischer traces two decades of automotive security research, noting that the first published car hack and the first Arduino both appeared in 2005—the same year as early Confidence work. He surveys people, papers, hardware, and community milestones that shaped modern vehicle exploitation.

CAN bus fundamentals

Unlike IP networks with explicit senders and receivers, CAN is message-based: every controller broadcasts and listens. That broadcast model makes packet injection and recording powerful, and requires reliable mechanisms to drop or ignore unwanted frames when collisions occur.

Community tools and conversions

Fischer highlights builders like Jack Richard, who converted petrol cars to electric platforms and ran workshops on EV conversions using lead-acid battery packs. He also covers classic research demonstrating CAN capture and replay, explaining why those techniques remain relevant for today's connected vehicles.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Security researcher Thomas Fischer delivers a retrospective on the twenty-year evolution of automotive hacking and in-vehicle network exploitation at the Confidence conference. Marking two decades since early published automotive vulnerabilities and the inception of the Arduino platform in 2005, Fischer traces the development of car hacking hardware, protocols, and adversary techniques. He explores the mechanics of in-vehicle communications across CAN and LIN buses, reviews open-source hardware tools, and analyzes modern theft vectors including CAN injection attacks and emerging electric vehicle (EV) charging surfaces.

Key Topics:
- Two decades of automotive security evolution: from early Arduino interfaces to modern connected vehicles
- In-vehicle network architectures: Controller Area Network (CAN bus), LIN bus, and gateway ECUs
- Evolution of open-source automotive hacking hardware (Panda, Carloop, Macchina M2, Comma.ai)
- Real-world attack vectors: CAN injection theft via headlamp wiring harnesses and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) risks

Technical Details:
Fischer outlines the technical foundations that make automotive systems accessible to security researchers, beginning with mandatory OBD-II diagnostic ports originally legislated for emissions testing. In modern vehicles, Electronic Control Units (ECUs) communicate across multiple multiplexed networks. The primary backbone is the Controller Area Network (CAN bus), a message-based broadcast protocol utilizing differential signaling without inherent cryptographic authentication or source addressing. Low-speed, cost-sensitive peripheral components (such as power windows, door locks, and side mirrors) typically utilize Local Interconnect Network (LIN) bus interfaces, which simplify wiring complexity. Central gateway ECUs route and filter messages between isolated domains (e.g., separating body control modules from the safety-critical engine and powertrain bus).

The speaker details the progression of automotive research tooling over the past twenty years. Early practitioners built custom CAN shields on first-generation Arduinos; this evolved into specialized, community-driven platforms such as the Macchina M2 (a modular board featuring dual CAN transceivers, single-wire CAN, and LIN capabilities), Freematics, and the Comma.ai Panda (an OBD-to-USB interface integrated with OpenPilot for autonomous driving research). Fischer explains modern physical exploitation techniques, notably "CAN injection" attacks widely adopted by car thieves targeting Japanese and European vehicles. Perpetrators pry away external front bumper panels or wheel arches to access exposed headlight wiring harnesses directly connected to the vehicle's CAN bus. By connecting a small spoofing device directly to the wiring, attackers inject fraudulent CAN frames impersonating keyless entry authorization modules, instructing the central gateway to unlock the doors and start the ignition without physical keys. Finally, Fischer highlights new vectors in electric vehicles, where Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) power interfaces (ISO 15118) combine high-voltage charging with bidirectional data communications, bridging vehicle internal buses with electrical grid infrastructure.

Key Takeaways:
Automotive manufacturers must deprecate plaintext, unauthenticated internal bus architectures in favor of cryptographically authenticated messaging (such as Secure Onboard Communication / SecOC) across all CAN networks. Central gateway ECUs must strictly validate message provenance and isolate exterior wiring harnesses—such as headlight modules—from safety and access control buses to eliminate CAN injection vulnerabilities. As connected and electric vehicles integrate vehicle-to-grid interfaces and over-the-air (OTA) updates, security teams must treat physical vehicle connectors as exposed network perimeters requiring robust mutual authentication.

talks.title: Tomer Peled - Abusing VBS enclaves to create evasive malware
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Tomer Peled - Abusing VBS enclaves to create evasive malware.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Tomer Peled presents joint research conducted with Ori David from the Akamai Security Group exploring Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) and VBS enclaves in Windows. Peled details how VBS relies on Hyper-V to create isolated Virtual Trust Levels (VTLs), moving beyond traditional ring 3 and ring 0 boundaries to counter kernel exploits and Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) tactics. While VBS enclaves are designed to protect sensitive process data and cryptographic routines inside an isolated user mode, Peled examines how attackers can abuse these same trust boundaries to evade Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) systems.

### Key Topics
- **Virtualization-Based Security (VBS) Architecture**: From Windows 11 onward, Windows runs above Hyper-V. The architecture separates normal execution (VTL0, containing ring 3 user mode and ring 0 kernel mode) from higher-privileged execution (VTL1, containing the secure kernel and isolated user mode). VTL0 cannot read or write to VTL1.
- **VBS Enclaves**: Enclaves compile as DLLs and run inside VTL1's isolated user mode. Unlike normal processes that load `ntdll.dll` (which EDRs routinely hook in user and kernel mode), enclaves load `vertdll.dll` to interact with the secure kernel, meaning enclave API calls bypass EDR hooks entirely.
- **Bypassing Microsoft Enclave Signing Constraints**: VBS enclaves must be signed by Microsoft. Peled explores four potential attack paths to navigate this barrier: acquiring valid signatures via stolen certificates or shell companies; exploiting the enclave loading mechanism (referencing Alex Ionescu's 2024 vulnerability); leveraging debuggable enclaves; and adopting a Bring Your Own Vulnerable Enclave (BYOVE) model.
- **Debuggable Enclaves**: Debugging enclaves in VTL1 from VTL0 debuggers is enabled by a specific flag implemented via secure kernel exceptions. If an attacker obtains a debuggable enclave, they can load it, locate an enclave routine via `GetProcAddress`, adjust memory permissions using `VirtualProtect` to `PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE`, write shellcode, and invoke it directly in isolated user mode.
- **Bring Your Own Vulnerable Enclave & Mirage**: Analyzing CVE-2023-36880 (an information disclosure issue in Microsoft Edge discovered by Alex Gao), the researchers found a proof-of-concept providing an arbitrary read/write primitive into an enclave. Because Arbitrary Code Guard (ACG) prevents dynamic code allocation inside the enclave itself, the researchers instead developed "Mirage," a sleep obfuscation technique and tool.

### Technical Details & Mirage Demonstration
Mirage leverages the arbitrary read/write primitive between VTL0 and VTL1 to evade memory scanners:
1. A VTL0 process stages malicious shellcode by writing it directly into the enclave inside VTL1.
2. While dormant in the sleep phase, the VTL0 buffer is zeroed out, leaving no detectable artifacts in normal process memory for EDRs to scan.
3. When execution is required, the enclave writes the shellcode back into the VTL0 buffer. Because operations originating from VTL1 cannot be inspected or hooked by VTL0 EDRs, this write operation succeeds without interception.
4. The shellcode executes (demonstrated in the talk by launching `calc.exe`), after which the buffer is immediately overwritten with benign data (zeroes) and returns to sleep.

### Takeaways
VBS enclaves offer significant security isolation benefits, but they also present a compelling, unmonitored attack surface. Because enclaves communicate through `vertdll.dll` directly to the secure kernel, security tools currently lack visibility into VTL1. As adoption of enclaves increases, mechanisms such as sleep obfuscation through vulnerable enclaves (BYOVE) or misplaced debuggable enclaves represent practical avenues for stealthy malware execution. Peled urges security practitioners and blue teams to keep a close eye on enclaves as adoption grows.

talks.title: Bartosz Michalski - Quishing vs. User: The chase for the "un"scanned QR code
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Bartosz Michalski - Quishing vs. User: The chase for the "un"scanned QR code.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Bartosz Michalski, an analyst leading operations at the Cyber Security Operations Center (SOC) at Bank Pekao S.A. (with over 10,000 users), discusses quishing (QR code phishing) and analyzes the psychological and human dynamics involved in incident triage. Through a real-world case study of an employee who scanned a fraudulent QR code while working remotely, the presentation demonstrates why SOC teams must move away from penalizing users and instead cultivate psychological safety, direct communication, and comprehensive security awareness.

### Key Topics
- **Prevalence of Quishing**: Attackers increasingly deploy QR codes across physical locations (parking meters, charging stations, medical clinic bulletin boards) and digital channels (PDF email attachments pretending to come from brands like Microsoft, DHL, or DocuSign) to harvest credentials or infect systems.
- **The "Unscanned" QR Code Incident**: An incident investigation where SOC telemetry initially showed no trace of compromise, only for direct human communication to uncover that the user had scanned the QR code using a personal mobile device while working from home.
- **Human Emotion and Fear in Incident Reporting**: The fear of disciplinary action or job loss, especially among new or probationary staff, creates an urge to conceal mistakes or lie to security analysts, blinding defensive visibility.
- **The CyberPKO Education Program**: Development of proactive outreach initiatives to educate internal employees, corporate/retail clients, seniors, and younger generations.

### Technical Details
- **Email Security Limitations**: In the analyzed case, an employee received an inbound email containing a PDF titled "payment". Sender authentication mechanisms—SPF, DKIM, and DMARC—passed without issue, and the message did not trigger mass-mailing heuristics.
- **SOC Analysis Workflow**: An analyst manually identified the suspicious message, tested the URL and extracted QR code within a sandbox via a VNC session, and determined it redirected to a phishing landing page spoofing Microsoft credential authentication.
- **Mitigation & Telemetry Blind Spots**: The SOC blocked both the initial redirect URL and the final landing domain on proxy/Web Security Gateway systems, and blocked the sender address. Telemetry across corporate laptops and mobile devices showed zero visits to the malicious URLs.
- **Root Cause & Workarounds**: Investigation into SIEM and internal systems confirmed the user was working remotely. Direct phone outreach revealed the employee had scanned the code using a personal smartphone on their desk, bypassing corporate endpoint visibility. The user ultimately did not input credentials due to suspicion and familiarity with conditional access policies.

### Takeaways
- **Treat QR Codes as Untrusted Links**: Organizations and users must treat QR codes with the same skepticism as unsolicited links, validating source legitimacy before scanning.
- **Avoid Stigmatizing Mistakes**: Security teams must adopt a calm, supportive approach when speaking with users. Establishing trust and reassuring users that their honesty protects the entire organization prevents employees from lying about security lapses.
- **Visible, Accessible SOC Outreach**: Clear reporting pathways (Outlook reporting buttons, ticketing systems, direct hotlines) combined with regular awareness sessions produce higher volumes of reporting and faster incident mitigation.
